newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: U.N. Yugoslavia war crimes tribunal - Key facts.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Yugoslavia war crimes tribunal - Key facts.

text.p: Following are the key facts about the U.N. war crimes tribunal for the former Yugoslavia.
* The International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia was established by Resolution 827 of the United Nations Security Council in May 1993.
* It is the first international body for the prosecution of war crimes since the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials held in the aftermath of World War Two.
* Resolution 827 stipulates that all states are obliged to cooperate fully with the tribunal.
* The tribunal has jurisdiction over individuals responsible for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity in the territory of the former Yugoslavia after January 1, 1991.
* It has no police force of its own and relies on the former Yugoslav republics, other states or the international peace force (SFOR) in Bosnia to make arrests.
* The tribunal consists of two trial chambers, each with three judges, and one appeals chamber with five judges.
* Judge Antonio Cassese of Italy is president of the tribunal. Louise Arbour of Canada is chief prosecutor.
* The tribunal may not try suspects in absentia, nor impose the death penalty. The maximum sentence is life imprisonment.
* As of May 7, 1997 the tribunal had indicted 75 suspects -- 54 Serbs, 18 Croats and three Moslems.
* A Bosnian Croat, Drazen Erdemovic, has been sentenced to 10 years in jail after confessing to killing unarmed Moslems at Srebrenica in 1995.
* A Bosnian Serb, Dusan Tadic, has been found guilty of persecution of Moslems during a Serb "ethnic cleansing" campaign in Bosnia in 1992. He has not yet been sentenced.
* Six more men are in custody in the tribunal's 24-cell detention centre awaiting trial.
* The two most prominent indicted suspects are former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and former Bosnian Serb military commander General Ratko Mladic, both of whom remain at large.
